title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
description: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major drive
body: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy."In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took."If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues."With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs."The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week."The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

schema.headline: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?

title: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere
description: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock Image source, Zainab JiwaImage caption, Zendaya's reaction to Zainab's outfi
body: Zendaya saw me on the red carpet and her jaw dropped - I'm still in shock Image source, Zainab JiwaImage caption, Zendaya's reaction to Zainab's outfit got 19m TikTok viewsByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent"I can't zip this! Mummm?"This was 29-year-old Zainab Jiwa, calling out for help squeezing into a corset while filming a "get-ready-with-me" TikTok video. It's a scene many 20-somethings still living at home will relate to.The difference is, Zainab was on her way to the recent London premiere of The Odyssey, one of the summer's biggest blockbusters.She was invited there as a guest and says she caught the eye of Hollywood megastar Zendaya, thanks to her custom look: a striking gold gown complete with a hood."She just walked past, and she saw me there. Her jaw just dropped, so did mine," Zainab tells me."It was just a stare-off for a minute, and she was like, 'Oh my god, amazing, amazing,' and then she just walked off.""I’m still in shock,” she adds. “The thought of her noticing my outfit blew my mind."The interaction went viral, external with 19m TikTok views. Her phone blew up.While Zendaya has been ruling the red carpets with high-fashion "method dressing" – where stars match outfits to a film's themes – Zainab is perhaps proving that independent creators like her can give Hollywood a run for its money.Zainab, who is Muslim and wears a hijab, is also often one of the only people covering her hair at premieres, but she says finding ways to incorporate modest wear is part of the fun."Even though you're covered, you can still find a way to be on theme.”Image source, Dave Benett-WireImage/Getty Images/HBO Max UKArriving for our interview at BBC Broadcasting House this week, her look was on-point in an olive shirt, tie, and brooches. "I put in effort today," she says.She's a self-confessed fashion addict. "From the womb," she says, when I ask her when her passion started.Her other love is film - but she initially kept that as a hobby. Still, she posted videos on social media for fun about her favourite films and outfits inspired by them.Soon, major studios took notice. Disney was first, offering her a junket interview for the series Moon Knight, where she got to interview the stars."I thought it was a scam,” she says. “I can’t watch that back. I was NOT good.”Image source, Jeff Spicer/ Getty Images for Sony PicturesToday, Zainab is a full-time creator and presenter, interviewing A-listers such as Denzel Washington, Paul Mescal, Tom Hiddleston and Zendaya herself – while decked head to toe in outfits paying homage to the films.She's one of many digital content creators on the red carpet, with others including Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg, Reece Feldman and social media personality Jake Shane.It's not always easy. Sometimes, Zainab gets invites to premieres the night before, meaning a mad rush to sort her look before travelling to the event - often by public transport (“and I look ridiculous”).She works with a range of designers and brands, but says she also keeps costs down by reusing items as much as possible.Her outfits are purposely bold, allowing her to "break the ice" with stars. For House of the Dragon season two, she wore a red gown by a student designer featuring three faces wearing hijabs."I'm a bit extra, but I like to add culture in everything I do," she says.For Spider-Man: Brand New Day, she customised her look with spiderweb henna. For Gladiator II, she wore gold armour.Image source, Simon Ackerman/FilmMagicShe admits she has worried whether dressing modestly will make it harder for her to succeed in this industry, but she finds pleasure in it too."I have a fun time working around the fact that I cover my hair or I cover my arms," she says. "I'd call it halalify the look. I'd always say, ‘'but how do I halalify this?'""I enjoy that bit the most because it shows there's no restriction really here."But while Zainab spends much of her time rubbing shoulders with Hollywood royalty, home life in Harrow, north-west London is completely different."Oh my god, my house is chaos," she laughs. Storage space is at a premium, and outfits often end up "shoved somewhere".She has a cat, siblings who often pop in, and parents who are frequently enlisted for wardrobe emergencies.Despite it not being the career trajectory they’d expected for their daughter, Zainab says her parents are now "so supportive".Image source, Walt Disney Ltd/BAFTA/Paramount Pictures/WireImage via Getty ImagesWith 660,000 followers on TikTok and close to 400,000 on Instagram, she's becoming a key content creator in this field. But she also faces criticism - including from some who claim her outfits are not modest enough."There's always hate in this industry," she says. But she adds: "For every negative comment, there's so many positive ones."If I'm doing it to inspire other people, or entertain other people, or educate other people, if that's still happening, then I really don't care about the rest."For now though, Zainab is swept up in enjoying a string of blockbusters."The summer's felt good for film - I think it's exciting," she says."And there's loads more coming. We've got Dune. We've got Doomsday," she says."I love film and TV. I think it's a really fun way to build community," she adds. "I'm just a fan. At the end of the day, I'm just a fan."

schema.headline: Zainab Jiwa: My viral moment with Zendaya at The Odyssey premiere

title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
description: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled
body: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain."This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

schema.headline: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast

title: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss returning to Ireland amid tight security
description: The Irish government jet carrying suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan has departed Dubai for Dublin.The 49-year-old was arrested in the United Arab Em
body: The Irish government jet carrying suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan has departed Dubai for Dublin.The 49-year-old was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April and is being extradited to the Republic of Ireland to face a charge of directing a criminal organisation.Kinahan will be immediately charged upon his arrival in Dublin and then brought by gardaí (Irish police) to appear before the non-jury, three judge Special Criminal Court on Sunday evening.A large-scale security operation is in place. Ahead of the extradition the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.According to flight tracking data, the plane carrying Kinahan departed Dubai at 13:19 local time and is expected to land in Dublin before 19:00 local time on Sunday.Irish authorities are expected to prosecute him for his involvement in leading an organised crime group.The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.Kinahan is not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.The US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after he and other members of his family were identified as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss returning to Ireland amid tight security

title: Family of Kaylan Hippsley devastated as killer Harley Whiteman to be freed early
description: Julie Craig, Kaylan's cousin, said the news had left the family "devastated".She said they had received a phone call from the victim support team two
body: Julie Craig, Kaylan's cousin, said the news had left the family "devastated".She said they had received a phone call from the victim support team two weeks ago, informing them there was going to be a change to Whiteman's prison conditions."We've had a letter from the prison service, saying his sentence is being reviewed as part of the Sentencing Act 2026, where there's been a remodel, and as a result of that his sentence has been reduced to four years, of which he has to serve at least half," Craig said. She said this meant Whiteman could be released under licence in the autumn."It beggar's belief that after two years he's allowed back into the community," she said."It's absolutely devastating. Kaylan's grandmother, who is his legal guardian, she is absolutely distraught. She's been unable to return to the home she shared with him."This just feels like a kick in the teeth."Craig said she wanted the decision to be reversed."I understand there needs to be changes because the prisons are full to capacity. But that's not the victims' fault," she said."Harley Whiteman will come out, he'll have the rest of his life to live."But Kaylan was only 13. I want them to take that into consideration when they're making these decisions. It's just wrong."If it means building new prisons, then that's what they need to do."She said the family "promised" Kaylan they would get justice for him, and had started a petition calling for Whiteman to be denied early release from prison.A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said it wanted to "block more offenders from getting out sooner into their sentence", but that could not happen without "risking prisons reaching capacity and collapsing"."If that happened, police could not make arrests, courts could not remand offenders and there would be unchecked criminality on our streets," it added."We are pulling every lever to protect the public and cut crime – building prison places at the fastest rate since the Victorian era, launching the biggest ever expansion of tagging to toughen community punishment and increasing support to victims, giving them a say in the strict licence conditions of offenders."

schema.headline: Family of Kaylan Hippsley devastated as killer Harley Whiteman to be freed early

title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
description: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge
body: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge SandemanOn Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, The view towards the sky from the hill in Galicia where Mark hopes to capture the total eclipseHe's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.But this is his first total solar eclipse."I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him."I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory Phillips-Brown flew from upstate New York to Iceland to see the eclipseThis will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago."It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomenon more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation."They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory booked their flights and camper van more than a year agoThe path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says."What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew."We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."Image source, Andrew WillsImage caption, Andrew Wills is travelling to Majorca with his wife and 90-year-old father to see the eclipseHe has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon."We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago."We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer."And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph."We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

schema.headline: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world

title: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites
description: Image source, ReutersBySebastian Usherglobal affairs correspondent, and Callum TulleyReporting fromin Sebastia, occupied West BankUp in the hills abov
body: Image source, ReutersBySebastian Usherglobal affairs correspondent, and Callum TulleyReporting fromin Sebastia, occupied West BankUp in the hills above the Roman columns of the ancient site of Sebastia, in the occupied West Bank, are olive fields that have been cultivated for generations by Palestinian families.One of the landowners, Abu Mudif, says he has received notification that his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres that the Israeli authorities are taking possession of in order, they say, to protect and develop the site for a major new national park.Typically, Palestinian landowners receive little or no payment for such land expropriation. And even when it is offered, most refuse it as they see accepting it as giving recognition and legitimacy to the loss of what they see as their patrimony.It's a vital income for Abu Mudif to lose of course, but it goes deeper than that for him.Image caption, Abu Mudif says his land is part of a tranche of about 450 acres being expropriated by Israeli authorities"If I wanted to describe it, the closest description I can give is that it is like having your soul ripped away. I cannot imagine myself without my land."Nahed Sakha owns a local restaurant that is under threat of demolition.He says the Israeli plan seems to be to cut Palestinian residents off from the archaeological site, which dates back thousands of years and has significant remains from the ancient Jewish past, as well as many other eras including the Romans, the Crusaders and the Ottomans."Restoration work has now begun along with excavations," he says. "Landowners were told that no-one would be allowed to use or plough their land."Image caption, Unesco added Sebastia to its World Heritage List on 25 July following an emergency procedureThe concerns of the village that surrounds Sebastia have been echoed by the United Nations culture and education agency, Unesco, which has now declared it not just a World Heritage Site but also added it to the List of World Heritage in Danger.Unesco says that the main threat facing the site concerns what it calls the "planned expropriation and creation of the 'Samaria' (Shomron) national park, which could divide the property".Standing on a path between the entrance car park in Sebastia on one side - where the Roman-era forum once stood - and the columns of the basilica on the other, the village mayor, Mohammed Azem, looks down to his right at some rubbish left in the ruins.He says locals are now worried about reaching down to clean the area as it might cause problems with Israeli security forces and settlers.The path on which he stands divides the site between Area B of the West Bank - which is under Palestinian civil and Israeli security control - and Area C, which is under full Israeli civil and security control.Last week, Israel allocated roughly 113 million shekels (£27.8m), external to expanding its control over archaeological sites in the West Bank. Some projects involve sites in areas administered by the Palestinian Authority.Image caption, The Cathedral of St John the Baptist/Mosque of Nabi Yahya is part of the Unesco-listed siteIn the remains of the Roman theatre, Israeli activist Alon Arad - who heads Emek Shaveh, an Israeli group that aims to ensure that the ancient heritage of the region belongs to all communities - says that the Israeli authorities have bypassed consultation with the local administration and residents of Sebastia."The thing is that Israel is not the owner of this place. This is a Palestinian heritage site. And in order to develop it in a positive way, it has to be done with the local community, with the municipality, so they can benefit."The Israeli plans would see Sebastia's entrance moved to the other side of the vast site, away from the village and current car park and shops.The Palestinian tourism and foreign ministries have expressed their hope that recognition by Unesco may buttress international support for their opposition to Israeli land seizures in Sebastia.But the Israeli Foreign Minister, Gideon Saar, has portrayed Unesco's move as enabling Palestinian efforts to diminish historic Jewish ties to the West Bank."No vote in an international organisation can change history," he asserted.Image caption, Israeli activist Alon Arad says archaeology is being used as pretext by Israeli authorities to seize landFurther to the south in the West Bank and just in sight of Jerusalem is Herodium, a manmade hill with an extraordinary palace built on its summit by King Herod, who ruled the Kingdom of Judea just before the Christian era.Recently here, too, Israel has begun to expropriate land - this time about 80 acres - for what it says is the "preservation and development" of the site.Peace Now - an Israeli organisation that monitors settlements - says: "Under international law, as well as according to rulings of the Israeli Supreme Court, Israel is prohibited from expropriating land for settlement purposes or exclusively for the benefit of Israeli citizens"."Consequently, in order for the expropriation to be considered lawful, the state will likely argue that the site is intended to serve both Palestinian and Israeli populations, despite the apparent fact that its primary rationale and purpose are linked to settlement expansion and Israeli control."Image caption, Herodium is a hilltop fortress-palace close to BethlehemFor Shmuel Browns, who has worked on excavations in Herodium and leads deeply enthused guided tours, it's vital for Israeli archaeologists and officials to be able to oversee and protect places that are so freighted with historical and religious significance."Israel feels responsible to look after the archaeology, the artifacts, the history of this land," he says.But there has also been a drive to go further than this among far-right members of Israel's current government.A new law was proposed earlier this year that would have transferred control of archaeological sites to the Israeli heritage ministry from the Civil Administration, which operates under military authority, and given it sweeping powers to seize land for archaeological preservation across the West Bank.That bill passed its first reading in parliament in May but is now on hold as elections are coming up. It may never re-emerge.Image caption, Herodium guide Shmuel Browns says Israel feels responsible to look after local archaeologyBack in Sebastia, the Israeli activist Alon Arad says the very fact that the bill was put forward shows how archaeology itself has been weaponised in the West Bank."This is exactly how the mechanism works. You use archaeology, you use it in order to do excavations and to the narrative, to rewrite history, but you also use it in order to allocate lands or reallocate lands from Palestinian to Israeli," he warns.Increasingly, Palestinian residents of Sebastia fear that their close connection with the ruins is in danger of being lost.

schema.headline: Israel accused of weaponising archaeology at ancient West Bank sites

title: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing
description: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She
body: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes. For example, depending on available places:If I get AAA, then I could do physics at SussexBBC could be physics at AberystwythCCD could be physics at Nottingham TrentThe Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher. She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people. At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades". On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history. "The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says."That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day. That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade."You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says."Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact. "Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says."With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your results. But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website. "I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand. On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it."It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford. "All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available. "Work up a priority list," he says."For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person. She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities. "I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says."You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.

schema.headline: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing

title: Hot weather reveals hidden history across the South
description: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs
body: Image source, Pete SeawardImage caption, The outline of an 18th century garden is visible on a lawn at Blenheim PalaceByEthan GudgeSouth of EnglandAs the south of England continues to enjoy an unusually warm and dry summer, parch marks on lawns across the region have revealed the hidden histories of their location.Among the sites which have seen the outlines of historic installations exposed by the hot weather are Portchester Castle and Blenheim Palace.At Blenheim, the footprint of an 18th century garden - which had once stretched across the width of the entire palace - has revealed itself on a lawn.Andy Mills, the Unesco World Heritage Site's head gardener, told the BBC it was "absolutely magical" to see the outlines of the historic parterre - 260 years after it was demolished.Mills explained that the original parterre - which is a French word meaning 'on the ground' - had been constructed in 1705, and would have "cost an absolute fortune to install"."It was a very large extravagant thing to do, but it was a way of showing your wealth and importance and that sort of thing," he said.Image source, Blenheim PalaceImage caption, The original plans for the parterre at Blenheim show its scaleBut the garden was dismantled in 1760, only leaving its outline to be revealed in spells of particularly hot weather."The footprint of it has appeared out on the lawn, and it is absolutely fantastic - it's a huge structure, it's just massive," Mills said."We know it's there, we know it's under the ground, we know the archaeology is there and it's just one of those happy coincidences of this very, very hot weather that these things appear.""It's just superb to see - it's amazing."Image source, National TrustImage caption, The outlines of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames - have also been uncoveredElsewhere in Oxfordshire, the weather has also revealed the outline of some lost buildings at Greys Court - near Henley-on-Thames.The parch marks show a range of 16th century buildings which had once stood on the National Trust property's Oval Lawn.Archeological enquiries at the site in recent years have discovered that the outlines belonged to a long, narrow building which once stood on the lawn and linked two sides of a medieval courtyard.Image source, English HeritageImage caption, The footprint of a Tudor storehouse at Portchester Castle has been revealed by the warm weatherMeanwhile, at Portchester Castle in Hampshire, the warm conditions have led to parch marks revealing the outline of a Tudor storehouse.English Heritage, which runs the castle, said the storehouse was believed to date from between 1489 and 1540.Image source, National TrustImage caption, Parch marks at Mottisfont show the remains of 13th and 16th century wall foundationsMottisfont, near Romsey, has also experienced similar marks this summer - uncovering the remains of 13th and 16th century wall foundations.The National Trust said the walls were the "buried remains of monastery buildings including a cloister and various other buildings, as well as later Tudor alterations".Archaeologist James Brown said the outlines were "intriguing glimpses into the oldest history of buildings known" at Mottisfont."We have carried out some geophysical surveys but the buildings have never been dug so their secrets remain hidden except for these rare moments when their outlines appear in the lawns," he added.Get in touchYour Voice

title: What do Clacton by-election voters want from their next MP?
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The voters of Clacton are preparing to choose an MP for the sixth time in 12 yearsBySimon DedmanEssex political re
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The voters of Clacton are preparing to choose an MP for the sixth time in 12 yearsBySimon DedmanEssex political reporter in Clacton and Walton-on-the-NazeOn Thursday, Clacton goes to the polls for a by-election triggered by the resignation of Nigel Farage. What do voters have on their minds and what do they want from their next MP?There is more to the Clacton constituency than the town it is named after.The Essex parliamentary seat includes rural villages, thousands of hectares of farmland and several seaside towns and villages with glistening golden beaches including Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze.The forthcoming by-election was triggered by Farage's resignation from Parliament following questions and an investigation into his finances.The Reform UK leader has denied wrongdoing and said he wanted the people of Clacton to be "the judges of my actions".Thursday's poll will feature the largest number of candidates and the longest ballot paper in British electoral history.This will be the sixth time in the last 12 years that voters in this constituency have been asked to choose an MP.So what issues are they considering before placing their X in the box?Image source, BBC/Qays NajmImage caption, The seaside town of Walton-on-the-Naze is in the Clacton constituencyMany of the people who live in Walton and the wider constituency originate from east London. Their cuisine came, too.Tucking into pie, mash and liquor is the latest family to migrate to the Essex coast.  The Parmenters moved from Hornchurch last month."What I have seen around me is such friendly people, wherever you go," Pete Parmenter says over lunch in his new community.Image caption, Pete (left) and Debbie Parmenter moved last month to the Clacton constituencyThe family's experience of corridor care in both Essex and London hospitals is at the forefront of his wife Debbie's mind when politics comes up in conversation."We sat there all night waiting to be seen in a corridor and then were moved into a room where we had a chair," she says.Her son Nick, who is nearly 40, adds: "They just seemed completely overwhelmed, the hospitals. The wait times are huge so I'd rather they focus and spend money on fixing the NHS."But for Pete, the main issue is one that comes up a lot here: immigration.  "It's not 'kick all the immigrants out', but let's get a little bit more control of it.  That's probably a big issue for me and will guide me which way I actually vote when it comes to it."Image caption, Clyde Ellis-Hall says he "wants Britain to be Britain"On the table opposite, Clacton taxi driver Clyde Ellis-Hall agrees."I'm just not a left-wing person. I want Britain to be Britain, basically, and I want my kids and grandkids to grow up how I was brought up."If you go to all the main cities in the country now – London, Manchester, Birmingham – it's just totally changed."Image caption, Glenn White wants VAT cut for hospitality businessesGlenn White opened White's pie and mash shop in 1981 after moving from London. He turns 80 next year and plans to carry on serving and clearing tables.White says now is the hardest time he has known for running a small business."We still pay VAT at 20% and, as you know, it's a cheap meal in here. Government take over £1 for a meal [in tax]. That's my main gripe, really... struggling against the cost of running the shop."  White says he would like to see politicians cut VAT for hospitality as they did during the Covid pandemic when it was reduced to 5%.He says cafes and restaurants in Europe often pay lower VAT and thinks the French get a better deal from their government, where restaurants have a lower rate of VAT of 10% on non-alcoholic sales."The general worker will pay a much higher tax than an English worker," he says."But they get it back in the fact that their communities are nice places to live in. The pavements are all level, there's no potholes, and the government put that money back in."So when a French person wakes up in the morning, he walks out into a nice town. He doesn't trip over the paving stones; there's not lots of weeds growing up out the kerbs."  White feels this corner of England that he lives is not as well maintained and says people don't feel like they get back the tax they pay in.Clacton constituency factsAt 50, the average age of people here is 10 years older than the England averageA third of the working-age population is economically inactive – compared to fewer than one in five in the East of EnglandOne in four has a disability, compared to 17% in England20% of neighbourhoods in the Tendring district are highly deprived, of which most are around Clacton and JaywickSource: Office for National Statistics Image caption, Care home owner Rahul Jagota believes social care should be talked about more by politiciansThe health and social care sector employs 4,500 people in the Clacton constituency.  While the NHS, and access to GPs and dentists has been mentioned by many of the 34 candidates, social care has rarely featured."Social care is the biggest economy in the area. It's the most important economy in the area," says Rahul Jagota, who runs The Corner House care home in Clacton and is a former chair of the Essex Care Association. "We need our leaders to speak about it, speak about the issues, speak about what great work we do, be very positive about it and look at solutions," he says. "Why it's not on the agenda, I'm not sure, but it's pretty much recognised as we are the driving force of the local industry here."About 40% of his staff have come from abroad, with rest mainly local. Without foreign recruitment, there would have been staff shortages, he says.A full list of the candidates standing can be seen here.Get in touchDo you have a story suggestion for Essex?

title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happ
body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October."Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".

title: Why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many
description: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uni
body: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty."Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".They had been about to go on their honeymoon.But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers – Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole – will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more – at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.Some 6,000 prisoners had been due to be let out early under a law aimed at making space in the prisons system.Burnham paused that policy for a review after a public backlash, with particular focus on the possible release of two of PC Harper's killers after serving half rather than two-thirds of their sentences.But on Monday, while it was confirmed that about 1,000 prisoners would be excluded from the scheme, Bowers and Cole were not among them.Lissie described this as "disgraceful and disgusting", while PC Harper's mother said she was "devastated".A petition against their release has received more than 750,000 signatures.Long, the driver, is not eligible for early release.Recent weeks have shown just how much the case continues to stir strong emotions.Tiffany Lynch, chair of the National Police Federation of England and Wales, said that for rank and file officers up and down the country it "feels personal" – "there is disgust, upset"."We have a police officer who was four weeks into his marriage, dedicated to his job, responding to an incident of burglary, that our public expect of our police, has sacrificed his life in the line of duty and the people are not fulfilling their sentence," she said. "It just doesn't make sense."Stuart Blaik, the senior investigating officer in PC Harper's case, told BBC Breakfast his killers' early release was "particularly hard to understand" and would impact police morale.Justice Secretary Alex Norris has apologised to victims and their families and said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

title: How stray cats in Coventry made rave nights and pubs their home
description: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandiseImage source, Charly FuImage caption, Stray cat Fargo is proving an attraction f
body: Stray cats showing up at raves, gigs and pubs now have own merchandiseImage source, Charly FuImage caption, Stray cat Fargo is proving an attraction for ravers and gig-goersByVanessa PearceBBC News, West MidlandsCelebs pulling in punters with a club appearance is nothing new. But did they ever have so much fur?At venues in Coventry at least, the glitterati wear whiskers these days. It began when two stray cats made city venues their home, becoming social media stars thanks to the incongruous sights of tail and turntable, pint and paw.While one shows up at gigs and rave nights, the other is a bit more pub than dub. But each now has his own range of merch... and visitors flock for a glimpse of these meeow-vers and shakers.Murphy was first spotted living beneath a bush before wandering into the car park of The Old Windmill pub in the city centre, "rake thin" and in need of care. Now a permanent resident, he has become a firm favourite with customers."We've had people who've never been in the pub before, but have seen him on social media," said the venue's Peter Dunkley. "They come in and the first question is 'where's Murphy'?"Across town, Fargo is a well-known figure at Fargo Village, the creative hub after which he is named.  Regularly spotted around the site's shops and bars, he too has become an attraction in his own right, mixing among ravers and drinkers. Fargo Village staff have set up an Instagram account in an effort to track down his owner, and it has attracted a loyal following of fans eager to keep up with his daily adventures.Figure caption, Fargo and Murphy are credited with pulling in punters at Coventry venues."Loads of people come here just to see the cat," said Bernie Blossom, bar manager at Village venue The Box."He's such a darling, we've all fallen in love with him."Fargo first appeared around the site in October, Blossom said. "We were all outside the venue during Halloween and this black and white cat just kind of appeared, and started hanging out," she explained."Then over the next few months we'd see him at raves and late nights in The Box." And by the sound of it, Fargo just can't get enough of the vinyl...Image source, Alien She/David Nash/Instagram: CatcalledfargoImage caption, Fargo has become a regular at gigs at Just Dropped In "The cat's been coming to us for well over six months now," said Alun Roberts, owner of Just Dropped In record store."He started coming to some of our gigs, and would plop itself on to one of our seats."Fargo, however, is discerning."Some of the noisier gigs, some of the punk gigs, he's not so keen on," Roberts said. "He loves a bit of folk, a bit of ambient - [he's] not keen on drumming and stuff like that."Customers come in just to see where the cat is." Blossom said she had been searching for Fargo's owners, attaching a paper collar to him. "We saw him more and more and more over winter, until we kind of deducted that he might not have an owner because he was so dirty," she explained. Image caption, Murphy and Fargo each have their own line of merchandiseSarah Friedlos, owner of Beadlebop Design print studio said she had taken Fargo to a charity to check for a microchip, but with no luck. She also feeds him on a regular basis."He comes in here, has a good old scoff, and then a sleep and goes off for a bit," she said. "I had a few people in this morning who were just standing in the shop and pointing at something," she added. "I was like 'can I help you?' because I just forget he's there."A nickname has since emerged."We do call him Six-Dinners Sid because he gets fed in the record store, Beedlebop and The Box," Blossom said. Image source, CatcalledFargo/ Martha King SlayeImage caption, Businesses at Fargo Village are launching a range of merchandise to pay for vet billsStaff are launching a range of merchandise in order to pay for the cat's vet bills and wellbeing. Jo Taylor from the Village's Indie Mart said mugs, key rings, prints and badges were all being produced, using artwork created by Martha King Slaye. "We've had him checked over, but he'll need injections," she said. "He was neutered so he had an owner at some time," she added, "but in the six months he's been around he looks so much healthier.""He's so friendly with everyone, he's a joy to have around." Image source, The Old WindmillImage caption, Murphy the cat has helped raise money for Coventry FoodbankBack at The Old Windmill, Murphy merch is raising money for a good cause. Cat mugs sold in his name have raised about £80 for the Coventry Foodbank project "and there's more to come", Dunkley said. There are plans for how punters may start making donations to the RSPCA, with the venue acutely aware of animal welfare since its feline resident arrived."When he first moved in he hadn't been chipped or neutered, so that's all taken care of," Dunkley said.And it's proved mutually beneficial."As far as we're concerned," Dunkley explained, "Murphy does our marketing, and we pay him in food and accommodation, and the customers love him. "It's like hanging around with somebody who's really famous." Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Warwickshire
